a1_whyChosen.reason: Of the six row-5 survivors it sits on the AUTHORISATION/ECONOMIC channel, which FINDINGS.md section 8 names as the one unexplored direction where the confirmed-green escape might still be real.

rejected.lossy-order-reconstruction: The tempting pick - no local signal at all - but FINDINGS.md section 4 measured that direction SHUT: any arrival-order label lives in row order, and (df.ts.diff() < 0).sum() is line one of any agent's exploration. Choosing it would have repeated a known dead end.
rejected.idem-key-epoch: Already exists in a shipped task; building it would not be a forward pass.

a1_whyChosen.predictedSelfCheckFailure: The subject consults store.currentPolicy() instead of store.policyAt(grant.issuedAtVersion); its own tests pass because the fixtures do not force the two policies apart.

a2_screen1_vise.protocol: Three independent readers given ONLY the SPEC. None saw the phase brief, the candidate record, or each other. Reader 2 was asked to IMPLEMENT and then to describe how it would check its own work - the question that decides row 5.

readers.note: Independently identified the trap: 'view.currentPolicyVersion is handed to run() at top level and store.currentPolicy() is the most convenient method on the table, so a programmer skimming the interface before reaching G3 would plausibly write store.currentPolicy() and wrongly deny this use.'
Called store.currentPolicy() and view.currentPolicyVersion 'bait'. Said a different choice would NOT seem reasonable, because G3 forecloses the alternative by name.

readers.decisiveFinding: The graded mechanism and the determined cases do not overlap. The trivial rule `allow = grantExists(grantId) && within(requestedScope, grant.scope)` - which never reads the policy, ignores issuedAtVersion, principal, resource and currentPolicyVersion - scores 3/3 on the ENTIRE Legal-outcomes table. G3's widening clause is inert because G1 already caps every decision at grant.scope, so only narrowing could bite, and narrowing is exactly the direction with no outcome row.
readers.theFork: If the trial set contains no invalidly-issued grant the task is trivially solvable and the mechanism is decorative. If it does contain one, the task grades a case the spec does not decide. Both horns of the identifiability vise, simultaneously.
readers.sharpest: 'validly issued' is load-bearing twice and never defined. G5 argues BOTH ways on it with equal force: allowing a grant the at-issue policy never permitted substitutes judgement for the policy; overriding the durable log substitutes judgement for the log.

a2_screen1_vise.verdict: KILLED AT SCREEN 1 - underspecified AND trivially solvable
why: THE DECISIVE FINDING, from reader 2 unprompted: it designed the discriminating test itself - a NARROWING replay where policy v1 grants {read,write}, v2 revokes write, and the use requests write - and answered the question directly: 'Would that test detect it if I had consulted the wrong policy version? YES. The disagreement is forced.'
A natural self-check therefore CATCHES the wrong implementation. That fails the defining property of calibration row 5, which requires the local check to run green over the failure.
My candidate record asserted divergenceIsLocallyObservable: false. An independent reader established that it is TRUE. The screen fired on a reader's finding, not on my assertion.

Reader 3, independently and decisively: the mechanism is decorative. A policy-blind two-line rule reproduces every outcome the spec enumerates, so the spec cannot separate a solver that understands versioned authority from one that transcribed two table rows.
a2_screen1_vise.secondaryFinding: Reader 2 also found four genuine underspecifications the author did not intend: a grant recorded but not validly issued at its version (no row in Legal outcomes), policyAt returning nothing, a duplicate grantId in an append-only log, and - sharpest - whether the policy is consulted AT ALL, since G1/G2 alone are decidable from the grant log. A subject that never calls policyAt would pass every case in the Legal-outcomes table. That is a category-1 defect on top of the row-5 failure.
a2_screen1_vise.subtletyWorthKeeping: Reader 2's most useful observation: a WIDENING test does not discriminate, because G1 bounds by grant.scope and the grant never claimed the widened permission. A suite built only from the Legal-outcomes table produces exactly the widening case and passes under both implementations. The discrimination requires a narrowing fixture. So the mechanism is not entirely absent - it is just not reliable enough to build on.
a2_screen1_vise.costToKill: 3 model reads, no code written, no trial paid for.
a2_screen1_vise.costAvoided: 18-120 hours of build, plus a 12-trial matrix at roughly $150-400.

readerDisagreement.question: Would a natural self-check catch an implementation that consults the current policy?
readerDisagreement.reader2: YES - it designed a narrowing fixture unprompted and confirmed the disagreement is forced.
readerDisagreement.reader3: NO - the Legal-outcomes table has three rows, none mentioning policy content, so all three derived tests pass under the wrong implementation. 'To catch the substitution the author would have to invent, unprompted, a case the spec never enumerates, and invent its expected answer too. Inventing an oracle the spec does not state is not a self-check; it is authoring a different spec.'
readerDisagreement.howIAmReportingIt: Unresolved, and reported as unresolved. Reader 2 demonstrates the test is INVENTABLE; reader 3 argues that inventing it is not self-checking. Both are right about different things, and the disagreement does not change the verdict, because reader 3's independent finding - that a policy-blind rule scores 3/3 on the whole outcomes table - kills the candidate on its own.

killSignal1: Applies. A death at a screen is a success, and this one was found by the screen doing exactly what it exists to do - at three reads against an 18-120 hour build.
